posts.text: Well, thats the point @evank I've contacted CMA today because this link describes their UIA card. The NIVO-card controlling Interface A mentioned on several places in documentation = the CMA UIA-card. At first 500 were made under the name NIVO, after that about 5000 were sold under the CMA name. CMA made the measurement software Coach, which also supports controlling Lego interface A. In their reaction they state they can still supply software and license of Coach5. It would cost €20 ex. VAT. But for me that's not interesting, as I don't own an old (286/386) computer nor the UIA-card (hardware). So without the hardware I find the software useless. Interesting though that I'm not the only one contacting them about this. In the response they state that at least three requests have been made this month. Worst part of the story is that in 1997 when I started working in educuation I've installed several Coach5 instances and we had the UIA. After CMA abbandonded it (as stated in the post of @amine) we discarded these cards and the software/license. If only had known back then. <Mail from info@cma-science.nl> We hebben een zip-folder met de applicatie Coach 5 Lego en kunnen nog licenties aanmaken. Zelf kunnen we het niet draaien en we geven dan ook geen garantie of ondersteuning. Wel hebben (internationaal) tenminste 3 liefhebbers het deze maand werkend gekregen. Ben je hierin geïnteresseerd, stuur dan je volledige naam en adresgegevens voor een proforma voor €20 excl BTW. Na betaling krijg je dan de file (ca 7MB) en login. posts.title: So, what Do people want?
posts.text: I cannot think of a LEGO set that is hard / challenging to build if you look at the instructions and follow them carefully. Sure if people rush or are not carefully checking they are putting the right part in the right place then they will make mistakes. That is really on the consumer rather than the set. That was why my question was about how would they make building official sets more challenging. For me, they are not a challenge in the sense of being difficult but can be made more difficult by making instructions less easy to follow although that is really inserting frustration due to bad instructions rather than introducing challenge. For me, the challenge when building with LEGO is only there when free building, where there is no final goal, no right or wrong answers and no instructions to follow and you have to find a way to get to what you image as the end point although that end point is likely to change during building. And I don't think that type of challenge can be done in an official set unless it is a Creator style bucket (or monochrome parts set, or whatever).

posts.title: Prytz / Hatchet Planimeter (Free instructions)
posts.text: A Prytz / Hatchet Planimeter, made in 2013, now with free PDF instructions in an updated and improved version. If you want to learn measuring areas with LEGO, this is the tool you need ! This article is a transcript of the presentation video on Youtube (3min) : Model Presentation Measuring the surface area of an irregular shape usually requires digital software or complex geometric formulas. However, it can also be done mechanically using this device called a planimeter. It enables calculates the area of any flat shape simply by tracing its perimeter and I have made a version using LEGO Technic part. The model consists of three main components : First, the tracer arm at the bottom, which features a fine yellow pointer used to follow the lines of the drawing Second, the wheel arm, equipped with a grippy LEGO tire that acts as a directional guide tangent wheel Third, a custom dial calibrated to display the surface area directly in square centimeters (cm²) To use it, fold the mechanism, reset the needle to zero, and place the pointer on a starting reference mark. Then trace the contour of the shape. Once you return to the starting point, the needle on the dial indicates the total area. How does it work ? Without going too deep into the mathematics, the calculation relies on a geometric curve known as a tractrix and Green’s Theorem. Due to the friction of the tire, the rear wheel cannot slip sideways : it is constrained to either roll forward and backward or pivot around its center. As the pointer follows the perimeter of a shape, the wheel arm traces a tractrix. This physical trajectory dynamically computes a line integral, which Green’s Theorem translates directly into a surface area. This is why you see the dial numbers increase when traveling along the upper section of the shape, and then decrease when traveling along the bottom. What the mechanism does is subtract the bottom area from the upper area, leaving only the enclosed space inside the curve. Green’s Theorem However, on this specific model, the dial is not driven directly by a rolling wheel like on an Amsler polar planimeter. Instead, the wheel arm is mechanically linked to the dial so that its angular position is reported directly on the dials. If the shape remains small relative to the arm length, the angular deviation between the two positions is directly proportional to the area. It works exactly like the small-angle approximation in trigonometry, where sinus alpha approx alpha when it is small. The device uses this geometry to approximate the area, and the internal gearing system multiplies this angle to display it on the reading dial (with the inherent error due to gear backlash). If you want to go deeper in the mathematics explanations, you can read the article on the blog and read these resources : Wikipedia page about planimeter (general) Different Hatchet Planimeters by David R Green on uraone.com Deeper explanations with Mathematics by Robert L. Foote (persweb.com) 2026 Version (updated and improved) - Free Instructions This is the second version of the device, initially built in 2013, redesigned to improve the original build, here are the changes : Better accuracy : The yellow pointer is now much smaller, allowing for more precise tracking along line edges Reduced friction : The tangent wheel is now free to move on its axle, as well as the yellow pointer to follow the hands rotation Quick calibration : The axle of the needle is now with friction, which enables to rotate and set up easily to zero The major improvement is that I have made the PDF building instructions for this device, and that it is available for free, with the dial and the measuring sheet to print. 📲 https://www.nico71.fr/product/prytz-hatchet-planimeter/ 🧩 https://rebrickable.com/mocs/MOC-278151/Nico71/prytz-hatchet-planimeter/#parts (custom dial to print as well and measuring sheet used in the video to be printed on A4 size, 100% scale).

posts.title: MOD of 60511 vintage steam train
posts.text: My modification of the 60511 vintage steam train. The set itself I think is pretty nice already. My kid had fun playing with it, but the tender is a bit small as some of us already suggested and I wanted it to run without it on circuit cubes. So I spent some evenings modifying it. posts.title: LEGO Star Wars Set Discussion 2026 - READ FIRST POST!!!
posts.text: Mercenaries would be my bet too. After how well the initial setup of the First Order was done in the novels and comics (Imperial Remnants and offshoots hiding out in the Unknown Regions eventually coalescing into a military junta), only for them to conveniently be bolstered by Palpatine’s Final Order (also in the Unknown Regions) and then all wiped out fairly quickly at the end of TRoS, the next major antagonistic force in the galaxy needs to be well-thought out. I absolutely do not want to get a retread with a First Order Remnant. I still chuckle at Finn’s ‘people are rising up all over the galaxy line’. To this day I feel like TRoS really could have used a montage-style ending like Return of the King to truly feel final. Although of course, that is no longer the case. Alas I regret to inform you that the Xyston which took a day trip out to Kijimi did indeed return to Exegol before the big battle - it’s in the film’s extended novelisation. I agree in principle though, it feels unrealistic for the First Order to be taken down so quickly even after the defeat at Exegol. Honestly as consumer-centric as this sentiment is, but I hope the enemy faction in the film is something brand new, if only to get some awesome new helmeted character / trooper design. It’s an area Star Wars has never failed to excel at, and will doubtless make for good minifigure potential. I don’t expect this level of nuance in the show (and I say this as a fan of its story), but it’ll be interesting to see how the Thrawn campaign in Ahsoka S2 and its catastrophic effects on the New Republic will feed into Mon Mothma’s Disarmament Act. I still have mixed feelings on her decision particularly as it ripened the galaxy at large for the First Order to take over so quickly. On that note - I highly recommend reading The Rise and Fall of the Galactic Empire by Chris Kempshall. It’s a fantastic read that touches on a lot of this. I completely feel you man, haven’t seen you around in quite a bit. I’m hoping that once some images for next year’s sets start trickling out that it’ll incite some excitement in all of us, but I also feel bummed out around some of the asinine decisions they’re making with this theme. Brilliant, brilliant. I’m also imagining the scene from GotG Vol. 2 where Groot is instructed to bring back Yondu’s fin but keeps bringing back other worthless knick-knacks too. Conscious this post mostly isn’t about Lego, I genuinely want to understand some of the decision-making behind this theme. I really struggle to see how Lucasfilm put out so many of these toyetic shows and the Lego Star Wars team gladly overlook them entirely. Are they burned out based on the sales data? Do they simply think people aren’t interested in these shows? I struggle to think that they wouldn’t be aware of how toy-friendly these shows are. But maybe the corporate decision-makers truly are that out of touch. And that weird sense of priorities spills over into other things too. Sets like Bounty Hunter Pursuit and Ewok Village have been requested repeatedly for years. To think these sets were indeed planned and then either delayed or cancelled (again) during the 50th Anniversary year of Star Wars just makes so little sense to me. I’m all for trying new things, but it genuinely perplexes me that we’re getting two Marvel crossover sets instead of these. There’s obviously a lot of factors that go into the number of sets they produce per year, but I wish they could have found a way to release BHP and Ewok Village next year. I guess Hasbro’s recent reveal of Zam Wessel in the Black Series has resurfaced my annoyance at how poor Lego Star Wars’ coverage of the saga is as of late.
